"You will leave with a specification, not a prompt."

Last night

"Hello. I'd like to assess your English. Tell me about a memorable teaching experience."

answered live

"What do you think is the biggest problem in education today?"

answered live

"If you could change one thing about how learners are tested, what would it be?"

answered live
The placement interaction3:11 · scrub to the excerpt you want. Space plays and pauses while the player is focused.

Opening line: "I had this conversation last night. You'll hear its side. I'll give you mine."

This beat overruns in every rehearsal. Time your three answers. Twenty seconds each, hard stop.

Ask the room to note the evidence they hear — not the level they predict. You will come back to this exact sample in movement IV.

Ninety seconds later · the report
C1
verdict

"Your English is at C1, approaching C2. Wide vocabulary range, complex structures, strong coherence."

"To progress, work on your syntax and keep expanding your vocabulary."

The report appears — say nothing. Let them read C1.

Then the advice.

Then, live: "So I asked it why."

It's right.
And that is the problem.

It described the band. It never described me. That is not a diagnosis — it is a horoscope with a CEFR band on it.

Say "It's right." Then three full seconds of silence — count them. This closes the escape route: the critique can no longer be dismissed as a weak model.

"I'd give myself the same level. Accuracy is not my complaint."

Then the second half: "I asked it why, and it told me what the scale says. I asked what to do, and it told me to expand my vocabulary."

LAND: "That is a horoscope with a CEFR band on it." Advance immediately, no transition line.

Movement I · what a placement test is for
where

A defensible location on a scale

  • a cut score
  • a classification
  • a course-entry decision

Answered — and answered well.

why

A structured account of performance

  • attribute-level evidence
  • the misconception behind it
  • how uncertain the claim is
  • the next action

Unanswered — and never specified.

A diagnosis is not a measurement at lower resolution.

Alderson (2005), Diagnosing Foreign Language Proficiency. We kept building diagnostic tests by taking proficiency tests and making them shorter. A diagnosis is a different kind of claim, needing attributes specified before a single item is written.

"A placement test is engineered to be maximally informative at exactly one point — the cut score — and profoundly indifferent to everything either side of it."

"And it works. The problem is not that placement tests are bad. The problem is that we ask them a question they were never built to answer, and then treat the silence as the learner's fault."

"This is not a new complaint, and it is not an AI complaint. Alderson made it in 2005."

Do not attack placement tests. The design error is asking a sorting instrument for a diagnosis it was never specified to make.

Movement I · three jobs, routinely collapsed into one

A generated score is not evidence,
interpretation and decision at once.

1

Assessment

Collect evidence that can answer a declared question.

2

Evaluation

Interpret and weigh that evidence against a standard.

3

Decision

Assign a level, choose support, or trigger another task.

Name the question first. Specify the evidence. Then say who acts on the result, and how.

Distinction after New York State Education Department (2026), Evidence-Based Assessment Strategies webinar.

This distinction prevents the most common AI design error in the room: treating a generated score as though it were evidence, interpretation and decision simultaneously.

Ask: "For the last AI assessment you built — which of these three did the model actually do, and which did you quietly let it do?"

Movement I · every assessment answers three questions

Cognition

A model of competence. What is it we think the learner knows?

Observation

Tasks that elicit evidence of it.

Interpretation

The reasoning that turns a response into a claim.

Pellegrino, Chudowsky & Glaser (2001), Knowing What Students Know. National Research Council.

"Twenty-five years ago the National Research Council reduced it to three words."

Read each vertex. Pause after "response to claim."

"Every assessment answers all three — a placement test, an IELTS band, your own judgement in week three. They get answered whether or not the designer noticed."

"They are load-bearing together. Weaken one and the other two carry no weight."

Movement I · what generative AI actually changed

Cognition

No model of the learner arrives with the model.

unchanged

Observation

Prompts, variants, modalities and feedback drafts, at unprecedented speed.

transformed

Interpretation

No interpretive argument arrives with it either.

unchanged

One vertex inflated. Two untouched.

Not a weak model. A triangle with one corner.

Say it carefully: generative AI can support work at all three vertices. Its obvious, cheap gain is task production — which is why that is where everyone stopped. Do not quote an items-per-minute figure as a research statistic.

"So where did AI land? Here. Observation. Task generation."

"It is extraordinary at it. The most significant thing to happen to item production in my career. And it has done nothing, by itself, to the other two."

LAND: "One vertex inflated, two untouched. Not a weak model — a triangle with one corner."

Accuracy guard: if challenged, concede immediately that AI can assist at all three vertices; the point is that the default workflow exercises one.

Movement II · evidence-centred design
1

Student model

What claim do we want to make about this learner?

2

Evidence model

What observation would warrant that claim?

3

Task model

What task will produce that observation?

The item is built last.

Mislevy, Steinberg & Almond (2003), On the Structure of Educational Assessments. Built for computational assessment two decades before any of us had a language model.

"There is a framework that operationalises all three, and it was built for computational assessment two decades before any of us had a language model."

"The claim. Then the evidence that would warrant it. Only then the task."

LAND: "Notice the direction of travel. The item is the last thing you build, not the first."

Movement II · every prompt library I have ever seen
1

Student model

skipped
2

Evidence model

skipped
3

Task model

"Ten A2 questions on the past simple."

Nothing for the answers to be evidence of.

Read the prompt flatly. "Every prompt library, every workshop, every webinar I have sat through starts exactly there."

LAND: "That is a task-model request with no claim behind it. We didn't skip a step — we skipped the two steps that do the diagnosing."

"And I say that as someone who wrote prompts exactly like that for a year."

Movement II · a naming distinction worth keeping straight
canonical ECD

Three models

  • Student model
  • Evidence model
  • Task model

These organise the evidentiary argument. The literature is broader still — conceptual assessment framework, delivery architecture.

your six-field specification

Six fields

  • Claim  ·  Attributes
  • Task template  ·  Distractor rationale
  • Feedback and mediation  ·  Output schema

These operationalise the models for an AI workflow.

Call it an ECD-informed specification — not "the six models of ECD".

Mislevy, Almond & Lukas (2003), A Brief Introduction to Evidence-Centered Design. ETS RR-03-16.

Small slide, disproportionate credibility. The six blocks are a genuinely useful design artefact — they are not the canonical ontology, and someone in the room will know that.

Say it plainly and move on. Claiming less here lets you claim more later.

Movement II · the grain size of a claim
micro-claim

"Uses irregular past forms in a controlled completion task."

Evidence can come from one carefully specified item family.

level claim

"B2 spoken interaction overall."

Needs representative tasks, multiple attributes, an aggregation rule, standard setting, and a statement of uncertainty.

CEFR descriptors are independent criterion statements. A placement still requires an assessment argument.

Council of Europe (2020), CEFR Companion Volume, §2.8.

This slide is the guard rail for the worked item that comes next. One item demonstrates diagnostic reasoning at attribute level. It is not sufficient evidence for a CEFR placement, and you will say so before you show it.

"If you take one sentence home: match the size of your claim to the size of your evidence."

Movement II · confidence requires converging evidence

Same claim

Hold the CEFR-referenced interpretation steady.

Varied tasks

Conversation, selected response, writing, performance.

More than once

Stability across occasions — not one lucky or anxious moment.

Convergence

Does independent evidence support the same learner claim?

A new modality counts as a new measure only when it contributes non-redundant evidence.

The clinical analogy: a temperature alone does not justify a diagnosis. One item — even an authentic AI conversation — cannot carry a complete placement claim.

Vary the evidence source while holding the intended construct steady. That is also what lets you inspect transfer.

This is the slide that stops any single tool — yours included — from being asked to carry a whole decision.

Movement III · for feedback to change anything
1

Know the standard

Hold a concept of the quality being aimed for.

2

Compare to it

See the present performance against that standard.

3

Act to close the gap

Engage in action that moves the work toward it.

dies here

"Work on your syntax."

Sadler (1989). The three conditions are necessary and simultaneously satisfied — not a checklist worked through in sequence.

"AI is strong on the first two — it can state a standard beautifully and it can compare. It is weak on the third unless you design for it."

"'Work on your syntax' fails right here. Not because it's wrong — it's true — but because there is no action inside it."

Accuracy note: Sadler describes the three as simultaneous. Do not present them as a sequence.

Movement III · four levels of feedback

Task

Is this response correct?

almost all AI lives here

Process

What strategy or misconception produced it?

transfer happens here

Self-regulation

How can the learner check and correct next time?

transfer happens here

Self

What does this say about the person?

least useful for learning

Nothing prevents a language model operating in the middle two. Nobody asked it to.

Hattie & Timperley (2007). Task-level feedback is not inherently weak — it is powerful when it corrects faulty interpretations. The design target is a progression from task toward process and self-regulation.

"Task-level feedback is the cheapest to automate, which is why it is the only kind most tools produce."

Accuracy guard: do not say task feedback is weak. Say it is where tools stop. Hattie and Timperley are explicit that it helps when it corrects a faulty interpretation.

"So that is a design constraint we can write down."

A2 · past simple, irregular verbs · a micro-claim

Yesterday she ______ to the shop before it closed.

A · went

B · goed

C · gone

D · was going

Read the stem. "One item. Nothing remarkable."

Name each option. Slow down here — this is where the room starts writing.

Remind them of the previous slide: this supports a micro-claim, not a level.

A2 · every distractor carries an interpretation

Yesterday she ______ to the shop before it closed.

A · went

Target attribute demonstrated.

B · goed

Regular rule over-generalised. This learner has a rule.

C · gone

Participle substituted for simple past. Form without function.

D · was going

Aspect selected instead of tense. Not a tense error at all.

Four hypotheses about one learner.

Not one question with three wrong answers. No filler options, ever — every option must carry an evidentiary interpretation.

"B has the rule and over-applies it — that learner has learned something. C has the form but not the function. D isn't a tense error at all, it's aspect."

Ask the room: "Name the teaching response for B, C and D." Take three answers. They are three different lessons.

LAND: "This is not one question with three wrong answers. It is four hypotheses about one learner."

Movement III · what counts as evidence

"What a child can do with assistance today she will be able to do by herself tomorrow."

Independent

What the learner can do without help. The only thing a test measures.

Assisted

What becomes possible with graduated mediation.

Emerging

What the learner may later control alone.

Vygotsky (1978), Mind in Society, p. 87. Dynamic assessment operationalises the distinction; Poehner & Lantolf (2005) adapt it for the language classroom.

Use Vygotsky as the theoretical root — not as though he designed a scoring method.

"A conventional test is a photograph of the independent column. It deletes the other two by design."

Movement III · the learner gets it wrong — then we mediate
rung 1 · implicit

"Have another look at that sentence."

rung 2 · focused

"Something about the verb isn't right."

rung 3 · explicit

"'Go' is irregular. What's its past form?"

Log, every time

First successful rung  ·  the change in the response  ·  time to recovery  ·  evidence tag  ·  confidence

Poehner & Lantolf (2005). The rung is meaningful only if the ladder is standardised enough to support comparison, and logged with its response context.

"Now the part I actually came to say."

Read each rung in a teacher's voice, not a system's voice. Implicit. Less implicit. Explicit.

"You don't measure what the learner can do alone. You measure how much mediation they need — and you record which rung they needed."

The score is not the datum.
The rung is the datum.

Two learners both get it wrong. One recovers at rung one, one needs rung three. On a placement test they are identical. In a classroom they are nothing alike.

LAND the line, then give the two-learner example slowly.

AI doesn't make assessment faster.
It makes mediated assessment scalable.

Mediated assessment was always the most informative thing we do, and always the least scalable. It needed one expert mediator per learner, for as long as it took. So we didn't do it.

PEAK OF THE SESSION. Slow right down.

"A language model is a mediator." — then three seconds.

"Faster was never our problem. And we've spent two years using it to generate multiple-choice questions."

Movement IV

From a principle
to an instrument.

Everything so far is a claim about design. What follows is the test of it — a working unit, stage by stage, and where it still falls short.

Change of register. You stop arguing and start exhibiting.

"I'm going to walk you through one unit of something I built, and then show you where it isn't finished. Both halves matter."

Exhibit · one unit, five stages, a deliberate climb
DOK 1

Flashcards

Recognise the target lexis.

DOK 1

Comprehension

Locate stated information.

DOK 2

Grammar drill

Apply a rule in a controlled context.

DOK 2–4

Picture task

Locate, infer, transfer, extend.

DOK 3–4

Writing

Create — then reflect and rewrite.

Each rung changes what the response can be evidence of.

Nine units, gated in sequence. Recall evidence is cheap and reliable. Creation evidence is expensive and rich. A unit that stopped after stage three would be a quiz.

Walk the five briskly, fifteen seconds each. Designers recognise the shape immediately.

The argument: a DOK ladder is a task model with a competence model implied by it. Moving from recall to creation is not "getting harder" — it elicits a different class of evidence.

Stages 1–2 · DOK 1, recall and locate
Matching — recognitionTwelve cards, six pairs. Scored out of 20.
Selected response — comprehensionTen questions against one passage.

Necessary, reliable, and not sufficient. These two stages tell you what the learner has retained. Neither tells you how the learner thinks.

Move quickly. The room does not need convincing that flashcards test recall.

The one thing to say: "This is the layer most AI-generated assessment never leaves. It is the cheapest evidence to produce and the cheapest to score."

Stage 4 · one image, four cognitive demands
DOK 2–3 · infer and justify"Why do you think so?"
DOK 3 · transfer"…if you were with them?"
DOK 4 · extend"What would you like to learn?"

Question one asks where. The other three ask the learner to think, and to think in English.

Same image. Same vocabulary. Four different claims. The picture is not decoration — it is the shared referent that lets a low-level learner reason above their productive ceiling.

This is the slide that shows the ladder is real rather than labelled. Take it slowly.

"Question one is locate — a DOK 1 question with a picture. Question two asks for an inference and its warrant. Question three moves the learner into a hypothetical. Question four asks what they don't yet know, which is a metacognitive act."

Point out the pins: the learner places them on the image, so the evidence is anchored to something observable.

"Why do you
think so?"

Four words that change the construct. The learner is no longer demonstrating English — the learner is reasoning, and English is the vehicle carrying the reasoning where it can be observed.

Slow. This is the intellectual centre of the exhibit.

"A comprehension question asks the learner to find something I have already put in the text. This asks them to produce something that was never in the text — a judgement, and the grounds for it."

"That is why language teaching and thinking cannot be separated. Language is the only instrument we have for making thinking visible."

Guard: if asked whether A2 learners can do this — yes, at A2 length. The cognitive demand and the linguistic demand are independent dials. That is the whole point.

Metacognition I · attempt first, then compare
Unlocked only after all four are answered

The gate is the design

An exemplar shown before the attempt is a model to copy. Shown after, it is a standard to compare against. Same text, different assessment function.

"Compare and improve your own ideas"

Standard, comparison, action — Sadler's three conditions, sitting in the interface rather than in a rubric nobody reads.

"The learner has committed. Only now do they get to see a good answer — and they are told explicitly what to do with it."

Link back to Sadler. This is the slide where the theory and the product touch.

If asked whether this is just withholding help: no — it is sequencing help so that it produces reflection instead of imitation.

Stage 5 · DOK 4, creation
The extended task

An open task, tightly framed

Six to eight sentences, a named genre, a stated time frame — which is what makes past-tense control an observable attribute rather than a hope.

Constraints are the evidence model

Every constraint in the prompt is there because it makes one attribute visible in the response.

"Open tasks are not the opposite of specified tasks. The specification moves from the options into the constraints."

Ask the room: "What is 'in 6–8 sentences' actually doing?" Answer: it makes cohesion and range observable, and it makes the response comparable across learners.

Metacognition II · a model to reflect on, then the chance to rewrite
The improved copy — a model built from their own text"Read the improved copy well. Now it is your turn to rewrite."
Then the second attempt is offered, not imposedBoth the draft and the rewrite are kept.

Not a corrected script handed back. A better version of their own writing to study — and then the pen returned to them.

This is dynamic assessment in a product. The mediation is graduated — praise, then named criteria, then the model — and the learner acts after it, not instead of it.

Point at "Improved copy of your writing" and stress your. A generic exemplar teaches genre. A rewrite of the learner's own sentences teaches the gap between what they meant and what they wrote.

"And then it says: now it is your turn. The system does not keep the last word."

Link to the rung slide: this is rung three, offered after rungs one and two, and the learner's response to it is the datum.

Metacognition II · every correction carries its reason
Each correction names the rule behind it

Not this

"is → was"

This

"is → was — wrong tense choice. This task needs the past tense. Example: go → went."

Why it matters

The first corrects a token. The second names a misconception the learner can carry to the next task. Process level, not task level.

Hattie & Timperley (2007). The rule attached to the correction is what makes it transferable.

Short slide, one idea. "The correction is the cheap part. The rule is the expensive part, and it is the only part that transfers."

Tie back to the distractor slide: same principle, different stage — every judgement carries its interpretation with it.

Movement IV · the instrument the learner actually meets
One learner, one unit0:57 · the climb, start to finish.
The learner sees the whole ladderClick + to enlarge.

The four stages are the navigation

Flashcards, comprehension, pinpoint, writing. The learner can see where the demand is going before they get there, which is why the climb feels like a game rather than a test.

One score out of a hundred sits in the corner — and everything this session has argued is about what that number cannot carry. What the unit collects instead is on the next slide.

Under a minute — play it whole, say nothing over it.

Then enlarge the stage bar with the +. "Four stages, visible from the first screen. The learner is not being tested; they are climbing something they can see."

Point at Core: 0/100 and hold there for a beat, then move. "One number. Now look at what the unit actually gathered to arrive at it" — which is the five evidence types on the next slide.

Exhibit · why one unit uses five different task types
matching

Recognition

Is the form–meaning link there at all?

selected response

Discrimination

Can they choose between near options?

pin + open answer

Reasoning

Can they justify a judgement about something observable?

extended writing

Production

Can they sustain it across a whole text?

rewrite

Uptake

Can they act on mediation? This is the rung.

Five task types, one construct. Convergence is not variety for its own sake — each type answers a question the others cannot.

Callback to Movement II: a new modality counts as a new measure only when it contributes non-redundant evidence. Here each one does.

This is the slide that answers "why not just use one good task type?"

Walk the five and name what each one alone would miss. Spend longest on the fifth — uptake is the measure almost nobody collects, and this unit collects it for free.

LAND: "The fifth column is the one a placement test can never have. It requires a mediator."

Movement IV · personalised paths and branching scenarios

Branching is evidence-centred only when the
branch condition is an attribute.

not this

Difficulty-only adaptivity

  • score falls → serve an easier item
  • score rises → serve a harder one

A measurement optimisation. It finds the cut score faster. It diagnoses nothing.

this

Attribute-driven routing

  • response → rationale tag
  • tag → named attribute updated
  • attribute → next task chosen to test that

The student model selects the task. The path is the diagnosis being pursued.

Design rule: if you cannot name the learner variable a branch is conditioned on, the branch is entertainment, not assessment.

This is the slide that converts the theory into a build instruction. Spend time here.

"Ask of any branching scenario you have built: what is the condition on the arrow? If the answer is a number, you have an adaptive quiz. If it is a named misconception, you have a diagnosis."

Concede honestly: most branching in the wild — mine included, early on — is difficulty-only.

Movement IV · the test of the whole design

Can you click a score and walk backwards?

1

Item

The task, and the response given.

2

Rationale

The named misconception that option encodes.

3

Attribute

The learner variable it updates.

4

Claim

The CEFR-referenced statement, and its uncertainty.

A CEFR label without provenance is a conclusion without an argument.

Put your own product screenshot here if you have one. Walk backwards from a single placement decision to its evidence, live.

If a link is missing in your system, name it as the next design iteration rather than implying it exists. The room will respect that far more than a clean claim.

Movement IV · the loop, end to end
The adaptive test, and what reaches the teacher1:54 · the learner's side, then the teacher's side.
1

The test adapts

The next task is chosen from what the last response revealed, not from a running score.

2

The teacher receives evidence

Not a band and a percentage. A named account of what this learner did, and what to do on Sunday morning.

This is the whole argument, running once, end to end. Everything before it was the case for building it this way.

Play it through without narrating. Let them watch the learner's side, then the teacher's side.

Afterwards, one question to the room: "What did the teacher just receive that a placement report would not have given them?" Take two answers before you move on.

Space plays and pauses while the player is focused. The clip pauses itself when you leave the slide.

Movement IV · what the teacher actually receives
Where the learner isSkills reported separately, never merged into one figure.
And what to do about itFeedback, the learner's own words, placement and next action.

Every learner leaves with a paragraph written to them by name — and the teacher leaves with the row that explains it. Click the + on either half to read it full size.

Listening, reading, writing and speaking each carry their own score, their own feedback and their own evidence — and the learner's actual writing sits in the next column, so every claim can be checked against what they wrote.

Enlarge the right-hand half with the + and read one feedback cell aloud. Sultan's is the best one: it names what he did well, then gives one concrete next step with a worked example of the fix.

"Well done, three clear sentences, grammar accurate, ideas organised. Next: a capital letter for your name, and join two sentences with 'and' — like this." That is a standard, a comparison and an action, in a paragraph a child can act on."

Then the flags column: each one routes the teacher to a decision — a trial lesson, a book check, support at the .1 sublevel.

Before Friday: these are real learner names and ages on a public screen. Blur the first column or say you have permission.

Movement IV · the report a learner and a teacher actually receive
Speaking report — placement and aspect rubricsEvery band carries the utterance that warranted it.

Every claim shows its warrant

Range, accuracy, fluency, interaction, coherence — each banded separately, each with the learner's own words quoted underneath as the evidence.

The profile is not flat

Four aspects at A2, coherence at A1. That single dip is the teaching target, and a global "A2" would have erased it.

It states its own uncertainty

"Confidence: medium — calculated over 18 turns, 109 words." The report tells you how much evidence stands behind it.

This is the student model, made visible. Attributes named in advance, each warranted by observed performance, with the strength of the claim declared alongside it.

Slow down. This is the payoff of Movements II and III arriving in one screen.

Point at an evidence quotation. "That is the observation. The band above it is the interpretation. The report shows you both, which means you can disagree with it."

Then coherence at A1. "Four aspects agree and one does not. That disagreement is the most useful thing on the page."

Then confidence. "Eighteen turns, one hundred and nine words, medium confidence. Compare that with the tool at the start of this session, which gave me a level and no idea how sure it was."

Movement IV · and then it says what to do
Strengths, priorities, and a DOK-tagged action planEach focus block names the task and the level of thinking it demands.

Strengths quote the learner

"Evidence-based" is doing real work here: each strength names the turn it came from, so praise is checkable rather than generic.

Priorities are actions, not adjectives

Not "improve fluency". Expand turns into multi-clause sentences of twelve or more words using because, although, so that. That is Sadler's third condition satisfied.

The plan is DOK-laddered

Recall, apply, analyse — tagged explicitly. The report does not just say what to practise; it says at which level of demand.

Compare with the opening. "Work on your syntax" had no action inside it. Every block here names a task, a target, and a level.

This is the slide that closes the circle back to the cold open. Say so explicitly.

"Remember what I was told at the start: work on your syntax and keep expanding your vocabulary. Now read block one: another practice turn on this unit, answers of at least fifteen words. One of those is a horoscope. The other is a lesson plan."

The DOK tags matter to this room specifically — they are the same ladder from the game exhibit, applied to a speaking report.

Anonymity: the organization name has been masked from the action-plan heading. Check before you present.

Movement IV · retrieval, and what it does not buy you
retrieval can
  • retrieve the exact CEFR descriptor
  • retrieve rubrics and exemplars
  • retrieve the misconception map
  • return source-linked feedback
  • preserve an auditable evidence trail
retrieval cannot
  • define the construct
  • set a defensible cut score
  • create calibration data
  • establish fairness
  • own the educational consequence
log it

Record the retrieval set and the prompt version behind every consequential decision. When a descriptor changes, the trail must show which version supported the claim.

Gao et al. (2023/2024), RAG survey. The naive / advanced / modular paradigms are the literature's; the assessment reading of them is ours.

Introduce retrieval only now — after the assessment argument is clear. Earlier, and the room mistakes better grounding for better validity.

"The specification determines what should be retrieved and how the evidence is interpreted. Retrieval serves the design; it does not replace it."

If you want the taxonomy: naive grounds a single response, advanced retrieves richer evidence structures, modular routes the next task and logs provenance.

Movement V · three things the model does not get to do
1

Define the construct

What competence counts, and what is out of scope. The student model is a professional claim. Not delegable.

2

Set the standard

Familiarisation, specification, standardisation, empirical validation — every step is human judgement.

3

Own the consequence

Leave this up during questions — it signals the theory is sourced.

Likely Q1 — How do you validate generated items? → Kane, link two. Pilot, item statistics, discrimination indices. Say plainly it is unfinished work.

Likely Q2 — Isn't the mediation ladder just hints? → No. A hint helps; a recorded rung measures. The rung enters the profile as data.

Likely Q3 — Which tool was the assessor? → Name it. You ran a real session; nothing to hide.

Likely Q4 — Isn't gating the exemplar just withholding help? → No: the exemplar arrives at the moment it becomes a standard to compare against rather than a model to copy. Both are legitimate; they are different assessment functions.
